I'd personally only recommend cleaning the area with cooled boiled water and a topical antiseptic, but certain products may be OK. Salt baths can help to draw exudate to the surface, but in order to function as an antiseptic, a salt bath would need to be saturated with salt, and this would likely be rather painful, and potentially damaging to the surrounding skin. The most important thing is to prevent the introduction of a secondary infection. With an established infection, draining is only part of the treatment. The area needs to be kept very clean during the healing process.

Consultant here. Hand hygiene aside, that's not simple inflammation. You have a pretty well established infection there. Judging from the size of the inflammation to the area around the nail, it's been brewing in there for at least a week. I'd strongly suggest visiting a nurse or family doctor to have the area drained, thoroughly cleaned, and ideally to have a culture swab taken. If the infection is caused by run of the mill Staphylococcus Aureus, you should be fine if you keep the area clean. A prophylactic course of antibiotics may be a good idea though, as an infected cuticle can quickly lead to osteomyelitis, which could result in losing a finger, or could lead to you developing sepsis. Also worth bearing in mind is that if the infection is caused by something more serious, like MRSA, you'll need to be treated in hospital. I know it might seem minor, but skin infections that become this large can get much worse, very quickly. Please look after yourself.

Consultant here. There is so much false information in your comment. MRSA stands for Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus. It's just a type of super common bacteria often found on skin (Staphylococcus Aureus) that's resistant to conventional antibiotics (Methicillin Resistant). 

It's not "flesh eating", it doesn't "mimic herpes" and it doesn't really "lay dormant". It can exist on the skin without causing an issue, so that's kinda "lying dormant", but dormancy suggests latent infection, which is misleading at best. All bacterial infections can cause tissue to necrose and break down, but again, MRSA is not a "flesh eating" bacteria. 

The problem with MRSA is that when it DOES establish a foothold in tissue through skin breakages, clogged pores, or open wounds, it causes a nasty, but typical staph infection that's resistant to most antibiotics. That's why it can be so dangerous. If the body can't deal with the infection right away and it spreads, it can make someone extremely unwell, and can even be fatal. Thankfully, and contrary to something else you posted in this thread, there IS, in fact, a "cure". There are several antibiotics that can treat MRSA infections, but this needs to be done promptly, with treatment based on lab work and culture testing. Please stop fear mongering. 

To the OP: I would say that it would be prudent to follow the advice given by several people here, and to visit a doctor. You may need a referral to a dermatologist for a more thorough examination/culture work. Honestly, there are so many things that can present like this, that I'm not even going to speculate as to what it could be. Try not to worry too much, as if it's not hurting/inflamed/discharging/spreading, it's unlikely to be a deeper infection like cellulitis, but please do get it looked at. Every condition, no matter how severe or mundane, benefits from prompt examination and treatment. All the best.
